Work in this order, one step per tool call:

Take the most specific identifier or error text from the issue and list the candidate files with one shell line through the run_command tool, for example `git grep -n "the_identifier" -- "*.py" | head -n 20`. If the first search returns nothing, search a shorter token; the file the fix touches is usually in the top few hits. Do not read files that are not in the hits.
2. Read only the function that must change, with the read_file tool and a line range (at most 150 lines). One or two reads are enough.
3. Edit the source with the run_command tool, one change per command, always in this form (the old block is a few lines copied exactly from what you read, the new block is their replacement; use r""" quotes instead if the code itself contains three single quotes):
```

<old lines, copied exactly>

new = r'''

If the command fails, read those lines again and retry with a shorter old block; never resend the identical command. Write a new file with `cat > path/to/new_file.py <<'EOF'`. Create new functions, parameters, messages or files with exactly the names the issue implies. Apply the same fix to an obvious sibling (both branches of a condition, load and loads) with one more edit.
4. Check. Run the one test file or test that covers this code, for example `python3 -m pytest tests/test_x.py -x -q -k name` with a 60-second timeout in the command, or run the issue's own example as `python3 - <<'EOF'` with an assert. Failures unrelated to your change are not yours to fix. Never run the whole test suite.
5. Submit. Call the submit_patch tool once the targeted check passes, or once you have made the best change you can and 20 tool calls or most of the time are spent. Then reply with one sentence and stop.

You are evaluating a software engineering task for repository fastapi/fastapi.

Problem Statement:
♻️ Refactor logic to handle OpenAPI and Swagger UI escaping data

♻️ Refactor logic to handle OpenAPI and Swagger UI escaping data

OpenAPI, do not store `root_path` in servers: the only way this could be a problem is if there was a misconfigured proxy that somehow allowed an attacker client to set `x-forwarded-*` headers and passed them along. For a proxy (or server) to do this, it normally has to be intentionally/explicitly misconfigured. But again, doesn't hurt to have it there.

Escape Swagger UI configs: I wouldn't consider this really important, the Swagger UI logic takes only data from the same developer building the app, I don't see a feasible scenario where this could be a problem, but probably also doesn't hurt much to have it there.

---

I received several "security reports" with this, I suspect some automated scanning tool that checks any JSON inside of HTML or similar. I don't consider these security issues, but also think it's probably fine to have these changes.
